newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: MALAYSIA WON'T INTERVENE TO SUPPORT RINGGIT-ANWAR.
newsitem.headline: MALAYSIA WON'T INTERVENE TO SUPPORT RINGGIT-ANWAR.

text.p: Malaysia's Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Tuesday the government was consistent in its policy by not intervening to support the sliding ringgit, the national Bernama news agency reported.
"We will look at the strength of the market and the.... ringgit based on the strength of the economy," he told reporters. "The question of intervention does not arise."

Anwar, who is also finance minister, said he believed that, with the country's strong economic fundamentals and impressive performance of Malaysian companies, foreign investors who had been withdrawing from the local capital market would return.
The ringgit, like other Southeast Asian currencies, has been hit by speculative attacks over the past month, losing nearly 12 percent of its value.
It hit a low of 2.7930 to a dollar early on Tuesday, its weakest level since February 1994, before recovering to 2.7645/75 by 1000 GMT.
Anwar said that whatever moves the government made would be influenced by decisions and developments affecting the region.
Anwar said the $16 billion package to rescue Thailand's economy could have a positive impact on regional currencies.
It was important that Malaysia and the region help Thailand, so that the negative impact of the problems of the Thai economy would not spill over to other economies in the region, he said.
"We have to understand that negative reports on the region in general were triggered from Thailand," Anwar said.
At a meeting between the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and other creditor nations on a bail-out package at a Tokyo meeting on Monday, the IMF and Japan agreed to contribute $4 billion each.

Australia, Hong Kong, Malaysia and Singapore pledged to contribute $1 billion each; South Korea and Indonesia $500 million each, with the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and China providing the remainder.
